strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why categorical distributional RL can outperform expectation-based RL. The valid mixture decomposition and cross-entropy decomposition in Propositions 4.1–4.2 provide a potentially useful perspective for constructing critic-loss ablations.

The experiments cover eight Atari games and multiple continuous-control environments, include categorical and quantile-based critics, and investigate interactions with policy entropy. The observation that combining distributional critics and policy entropy can sometimes hurt performance is useful empirical evidence.

The manuscript discusses relevant prior work and honestly acknowledges the restriction of its theoretical analysis to CDRL and DERAC’s inconsistent performance advantages. The benchmark-based study presents no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central derivation of DERAC is incorrect. In Appendix I, writing δ = T^πQ_{θ*} − Q_θ, the squared augmented residual expands to E[δ²] + τE[H] + 2√τ E[δ√H]. Equation 36 writes a different cross term and then discards it. The invoked TD orthogonality does not hold for arbitrary learned critics and target networks. Consequently, Equation 10 is not established as equivalent to the proposed augmented Bellman objective.

The claimed exploration mechanism does not follow from decomposing the critic loss. Proposition 4.3 concerns idealized minimizers as bin width vanishes; it does not establish equivalent optimization dynamics under finite neural approximation or show that a mean-greedy policy seeks states with large distributional prediction errors. Furthermore, H(μ,q) = H(μ) + KL(μ||q), so cross-entropy remains positive and state-dependent even when q perfectly matches μ. Treating its magnitude as how far an estimate lags behind its target conflates irreducible return uncertainty with prediction error.

The policy-iteration guarantee does not establish convergence of the coupled learning procedure. Appendix H treats the entropy bonus as unchanged when replacing the old policy with the new policy, although the target return distribution depends on the policy and the estimated distribution changes during learning. Standard policy iteration applies if these quantities are frozen, but boundedness alone does not justify the claimed guarantee when they change.

The limiting argument connecting the decomposition to expectation-based RL requires additional care. For a regular continuous density, the mean-bin probability vanishes with bin width, forcing the admissible mixture coefficient toward one precisely where Proposition 4.3 takes its limit. The paper does not establish that this yields a useful equivalence for the full objective. Additionally, Appendix G’s own calculation gives a Wasserstein distance between Δ/4 and Δ/2, contradicting the claimed o(Δ) rate.

The experiments support performance differences but do not isolate their proposed cause. Changing target probabilities or switching between scalar and distributional critics also changes optimization and representation. There are no direct measurements of visitation, exploration coverage, or distributional prediction error, nor controlled experiments separating environmental randomness from learnable uncertainty. The IQN comparisons therefore cannot establish the proposed C51-specific mechanism, and empirical interpolation cannot substantiate the tabular convergence theorem as claimed in Section 6.2.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the supplied hyperparameter table and pseudocode. The experimental probability-transport parameter is not precisely mapped to the theoretical mixture coefficient, categorical support bounds and Atari training/evaluation settings are missing, and no implementation artifact is identified. The meaning of the shaded uncertainty bands is also unspecified. Together with the central theoretical gaps, these omissions outweigh the promising empirical observations.
